title: The Teachers Who Learned to Wait
subtitle: A science educator with a tape recorder found that teachers waited less than a second for an answer. What happened when they learned to wait three changed the room.

card.essence: Teachers who counted three seconds got longer, braver answers. The same silence, used by a speaker, sounds like control — and it is the cure for "um".

intention: you'll see why a short silence works better than a filler, use a two-second beat before you answer, and name how many points you will make so that you stop on time.
warmup: What do you do with your voice when you are not sure what to say next — and what do you think your listener hears?
How long is the longest silence you can comfortably leave in a conversation? Does it depend on who you are talking to?
Think of someone who sounds calm and in control when they speak. What do they do between sentences?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The teacher kept interrupting, so the student never finished a single answer.
items.meaning: interrupt — to start speaking while someone else is still speaking, so that they have to stop.

items.sent: The lesson was a rapid-fire series of short questions, with no time to think between them.
items.meaning: rapid-fire — coming one after another very quickly.

items.sent: After the longer pause, students gave more reasoned answers, using words like "because" and "so".
items.meaning: reasoned — based on clear thinking, with reasons given to support the idea.

items.sent: She spoke in a slow, deliberate way, choosing every word as if she had all day.
items.meaning: deliberate — done carefully and on purpose, without hurrying. (As a verb, deliberate means to think about something carefully before deciding.)

vocab.heading: B · Which expression fits?
vocab.intro: Say the expression you would use, then reveal.

items.sent: You need a few more seconds to work out your answer, so you say something that keeps the conversation going.
items.meaning: buy time — to delay a decision or answer so that you have longer to prepare.

items.sent: The question was not on the agenda, but she answered it clearly and confidently straight away.
items.meaning: think on your feet — to react quickly and sensibly to a situation without preparation.

items.sent: Some speakers say "you know" and "I mean" again and again because they cannot bear a quiet moment.
items.meaning: fill the silence — to say something, anything, so that there is no pause in the conversation.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: ___ a question  ·  ___ a concern  ·  ___ your voice
items.meaning: raise — to bring a topic up for discussion; also to make something higher or louder.

items.sent: set the ___  ·  keep ___ with someone  ·  at a steady ___
items.meaning: pace — the speed at which something happens or someone moves or speaks.

items.sent: lose your ___  ·  keep your ___  ·  regain your ___
items.meaning: composure — the ability to stay calm and controlled, especially in a difficult moment. The adjective is composed.

vocab_use: Tell me about the last time someone interrupted you. What did it do to your answer?
In which situation do you find it hardest to think on your feet?
What do you do when you need to buy time — and does it work?

story.heading: Part 1 — The tape recorder
paras: In the late 1960s, a science educator named Mary Budd Rowe began recording ordinary lessons in American classrooms. She was not interested in what was being taught. She wanted to know how the conversation actually worked, second by second.

She listened to hundreds of tapes and measured the gaps between speakers with a chart plotter. One number kept appearing. After a teacher asked a question, the average pause before someone answered was less than a second — in some of her measurements, about nine-tenths of one.

What happened next was predictable. If no answer arrived in time, the teacher rephrased the question, answered it, or moved to another student. Lessons became a fast series of short questions with very short answers.
checks: What did Rowe record, and what was she interested in?
What was the average pause after a teacher's question?
What did teachers do if the answer did not come quickly?
answers: Ordinary lessons in American classrooms. She wanted to know how the conversation worked — the timing, not the subject.
Less than a second — in some measurements about nine-tenths of a second.
They rephrased the question, answered it themselves or moved to another student.
story.discuss: Less than one second is very short. What can you actually do in a second when someone asks you a hard question?

story.heading: Part 2 — Three seconds
paras: Rowe then worked with teachers and asked them to try something simple: wait at least three seconds after asking a question, and wait again after a student had finished answering. Most of them found it uncomfortable. Three seconds of silence felt like a very long time.

She reported clear changes. Students' answers became longer and more reasoned. More students joined in, including quieter ones. Fewer replied "I don't know", and more asked questions of their own. The teachers changed as well: they asked fewer questions, and better ones.

She also noticed something less comfortable. Teachers gave the longest pause to the students they believed were strongest — on average about two seconds — and the shortest to those they believed were weakest. The silence was not neutral. It showed how much the teacher expected.
checks: What did Rowe ask teachers to do?
Name two changes she reported in the students' answers.
What did she notice about which students got the longest pause?
answers: To wait at least three seconds after a question — and again after an answer.
Any two: longer answers, more reasoned answers, more students taking part, fewer "I don't know" replies, more questions from the students.
Students the teacher thought were strongest got about two seconds; students thought to be weakest got the least.
story.discuss: Rowe's teachers found three seconds uncomfortable. When have you found a silence uncomfortable — and was it as long as it felt?

story.heading: Part 3 — What a silence tells people
paras: The research is old, and later studies have been more careful about what exactly changes and why. Some of the early claims were large, and most researchers would now describe the effect as real but modest. But the idea has stayed in teacher training around the world, because it works in practice: if you give people time, you often get better thinking.

Now turn the idea around. A speaker who pauses for two seconds before an answer gives a listener the same message: this question deserves to be answered properly. A speaker who rushes into the gap with "um", "so" and "you know" gives the opposite message — that they are looking for their thoughts in public.

The cruel part is that silence feels much longer to the person speaking than to the person listening. The nervous speaker hears a disaster; the listener hears someone thinking. Which of the two is correct? Mostly the listener — as long as the beat is short and the face stays calm.
checks: How do most researchers describe the effect today?
What message does a short pause give the listener?
Why does a silence feel worse to the speaker than to the listener?
answers: Real but modest — some early claims were bigger than later studies support.
That the question deserves a proper answer; it sounds composed, not lost.
Because time feels longer when you are the one who has to fill it; the listener simply hears someone thinking.
story.discuss: If a listener hears a short pause as thinking, why do so many speakers still rush to fill it? What are they afraid of?

tool_tab.lead: A beat is a short, deliberate silence — about two seconds. The tool is a loop of four moves that you repeat for every answer: think while the question finishes, take the beat, speak your point and say how many points you will make, then stop and let the silence close the answer.
how: Think: let the question finish. Never begin speaking before the other person has stopped.

Beat: count two seconds in your head — one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two. Look at the person, not at the ceiling. If it is a hard question, add one short phrase: Let me think about that for a moment.
Speak: give your point first. If there is more than one idea, name the number: Two things. You are now committed to a structure — and to a finish.
Stop: after your last word, stay silent for a beat. A clean stop is a full stop you can hear.

sort.intro: Each line comes from a real speaking situation. Is it a filler, a thinking phrase, a signpost or a clean stop? Choose, then check.

items.text: Um, so, yeah, basically, I mean, sort of…
items.why: words with no content that cover the silence; they show you are searching, not thinking.
it names a number, so you know the structure and the listener knows when you will finish.

items.text: That's a fair question — let me think about it for a moment.
items.why: it buys time in a way that sounds composed. Use one, then stop buying.
it ends the answer and signals that you have finished.

items.text: …so, you know, whatever, that's sort of it, I suppose.
items.why: it trails off; the listener cannot tell whether you have finished.

items.text: Give me a second to check that figure.
items.why: honest, short and specific; it is also true.

items.text: Three things, in this order: cost, timing, risk.
items.why: it names the number and the order of ideas before you say any of them.
a short, firm closing line; then stay quiet.

breaks: Video calls. On a weak connection a two-second silence can look like a frozen screen. Add one short phrase so they know you are still there: Let me think about that for a moment.
Different rhythms. People differ in how much silence feels comfortable between turns. Keep the beat, but adjust its length to the person in front of you.
A beat is not a freeze. Four or five seconds without any signal feels like a problem. If you need longer, say so: I'd like to come back to that. Can I get back to you by tomorrow?
discuss: Which part of the loop is hardest for you: the beat at the start or the silence at the end?
Is there a situation in which you should not leave a beat at all?

grammar.name: Signposting and parallel structure
grammar.lead: Naming a number commits you to a structure — and structure keeps sentences from getting lost. Two pieces of grammar do the work: signposting phrases at the start, and parallel structure inside the list.
notes: Signposts: There are two things I'd like to say. · Three points, briefly. · I have one concern and one suggestion. Then use sequencers that match: First… Second… Finally… or The first is… The second is…

Parallel structure: every item in a list must have the same grammatical shape. We need to reduce costs, improve quality and shorten delivery times. Not: …reduce costs, improving quality and a shorter delivery time. If you start with a verb, keep using verbs in the same form.
Thinking phrases (one at most): That's a fair question — let me think about it for a moment. · Before I answer, let me make sure I've understood. · Let me check that and come back to you.

exercises.heading: Keep it parallel
exercises.intro: Write the verb in brackets in the form that matches the rest of the list.
items: 1. Our priorities are reducing costs, improving quality and ___ (shorten) delivery times.
2. I want to explain the problem, ___ (propose) a solution and ask for your support.
3. The plan is simple: we test it, we fix it and we ___ (launch) it.
4. She is good at listening, asking questions and ___ (stay) calm.

exercises.heading: Choose the phrase
exercises.intro: Use each word from the box once: second · check · fair · make.
items: 1. That's a ___ question — let me think about it before I answer.
2. Before I answer, let me ___ sure I've understood what you're asking.
3. I'd rather not guess — let me ___ the figure and come back to you.
4. Two things. First, the cost. ___, the timing.

grammar.closing: Now answer a question of your own with a signpost: tell me how many things you will say, say them in parallel form, and stop.

speak.intro: Beat, point, number, stop. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “Let me think about that for a moment.” · “There are two things.” · “First… Second…” · “That's my view.” · “Before I answer, let me make sure I've understood.”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Beat, then point
paras: Choose one: Is it better to give bad news at once or to wait for the right moment? Should someone accept a promotion they are unsure about? Is a meeting ever better than an email? Before you answer, count two seconds in silence. Then give your point first, one reason, and stop.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Name the number
paras: Choose one: Three reasons people resist change. Two things that make a presentation memorable. Four habits of a good colleague. Say the number first, deliver exactly that many, and stop on the last word.

tasks.label: Task 3 — Teach the silence
paras: Explain Rowe's discovery to someone who has never heard of it, in sixty seconds. Open with a signpost — Two things happened… — and finish with a clean stop.

final: Is it more honest to say "um" or to stay silent? Does your answer change with the audience?
Rowe found that teachers gave less time to the students they expected least from. What do your own pauses say about who you expect to answer well?
When does a signpost help a listener, and when does it sound like a rehearsed trick?
From memory: explain the silent beat in four sentences, using buy time, fill the silence, composure and a signpost of your own.
